droplet.name: Building a Profile Generator
droplet.description: The droplet addresses the need to automate profile creation for Oasis club members at Northeastern University. Users will learn to design and construct the application's components and enhance its visual appeal through styling.
learningObjectives: Understand how to apply their knowledge of React and web development to turn an idea into a functional web project
Gain the ability to conceptualize and design a frontend application starting from an idea
Develop the skill to break down application designs into a series of manageable components
Learn to design data structures that suit the specific requirements of the application
Acquire proficiency in building diverse components to construct a fully functional web page
droplet.overview: This droplet guides users through the process of building a web application from scratch, assuming familiarity with code editors like VSCode, HTML, React, and JavaScript. The aim is to address a specific problem: creating profiles for new participants in a club at Northeastern University called Oasis. The manual creation of these profiles is deemed tedious, prompting the development of a web app to automate the process. Participants will learn how to design and construct the application, including necessary components, and explore styling to enhance the website's aesthetic appeal.

blocks.content:
We’ll be building a Profile Generator to solve the problem discussed above. Below is a screenshot of what we’re hoping to produce. Users enter information in the blue section and then click Generate!. Upon clicking, the green section appears. Here, we have a profile created for Frank.

Design

Before we begin coding, we want to figure out what components we need to build. Looking at our sample page, we can identify three essential components.

  • The form for users to input their information
  • The profile card that will appear after the “Generate!” button will be pressed.
  • The header at the top of the page providing information about the website

Setup

First, launch VS Code, setup your repo, and run create-react-app. If you need a refresher on VSCode or React setup, head back to the linked droplets.

We’ll start by creating components for each of our major sections. Create new files Header.js , Form.js, and Output.js in the “src” directory. Create an empty component in each file, leaving you with the following:

// Header.js

export default function Header() {
	return (
  	<>
  	</>
	)
}

// Form.js

export default function Form() {
	return (
  	<>
	</>
	)
}

// Output.js

export default function Output() {
	return (
	<>
	</>
	)
}

With these components, we’ll then head to the top level component in App.js. Here, we can use combine these components into one page.

// App.js
import Header from "./Header"; // import each of your 3 components
import Form from "./Form";
import Output from "./Output";

export default function App() {
	return (
    <div>
      <Header />
      <Form />
      <Output />
    </div>
  );
}

While we’re at it, let’s think about which components need access to which properties. We need four state variables to track values for each input in our form, and one to decide if the output should be shown. These can be added using the useState hook.

// App.js
import { useState } from "react"; // required to use state
import Header from "./Header"; // import each component
import Form from "./Form";
import Output from "./Output";

export default function App() {
  // input field values
  const [photo, setPhoto] = useState(null);
  const [name, setName] = useState("");
  const [title, setTitle] = useState("");
  const [fact, setFact] = useState("");

  // whether to show the output
  const [showOutput, setShowOutput] = useState(false);

  return (
    <div>
      <Header />
      <Form />
      <Output />
    </div>
  );
}

Not every variable needs to be passed to every component. The Form needs everything, but the Output only needs photo, name, title, and fact, and the Header doesn’t need anything. It is important to only provide each component the data it actually needs.

// App.js
import { useState } from "react"; // required to use state
import Header from "./Header"; // import each component
import Form from "./Form";
import Output from "./Output";

export default function App() {
  // input field values
  const [photo, setPhoto] = useState(null);
  const [name, setName] = useState("");
  const [title, setTitle] = useState("");
  const [fact, setFact] = useState("");
  
  // whether to show the output
  const [showOutput, setShowOutput] = useState(false);

  return (
    <div>
      <Header />
      <Form
		photo={photo} setPhoto={setPhoto}
		name={name} setName={setName}
		title={title} setTitle={setTitle}
		fact={fact} setFact={setFact}
		showOutput={showOutput} setShowOutput={setShowOutput}
	  />
      <Output photo={photo} name={name} title={title} fact={fact} />
    </div>
  );
}

For the form, we’ve provided all of our data, and all of the setters for our data. This will allow us to modify the data for the whole application from within the Form component. The output only needs the data, as it will not need to modify anything.

Header

The header is a quick component to set up. It contains only h1 and p elements:

export default function Header() {
  return (
    <>
      <h1>Profile Generator</h1>
      <p>Generate profile cards for Oasis members.</p>
    </>
  );
}

Form

To begin on the form, we need to give the component all of it’s arguments as they are passed in in the main component. This leaves us with a new empty component like this:

import React from "react";

export default function Form({
  photo,
  setPhoto,
  name,
  setName,
  title,
  setTitle,
  fact,
  setFact,
  showOutput,
  setShowOutput
}) {
  return (
	<>
	</>
  )
}

To create the form, we need to tell React what to do when the form is submitted. This can be accomplished by accessing the onSubmit event. Whenever an input with the type “submit” is selected, the code within the onSubmit will run.

// in Form.js

import React from "react";

export default function Form({
  photo,
  setPhoto,
  name,
  setName,
  title,
  setTitle,
  fact,
  setFact,
  showOutput,
  setShowOutput
}) {
  return (
	<div className="input">
      <form
        onSubmit={(e) => {
          e.preventDefault(); // stop submit from reloading the page
          setShowOutput(true); 
        }}
      >
	    {/* Inputs will go here! */}
	    <input type="submit" value="Generate!" />
      </form>
	</div>
  )
}

Now we can build out our inputs inside the form. For each input, we need to use onChange to tell React what to do when those input fields are modified. For each, we will use the appropriate setter passed in. We will also assign the input field’s value to the state value passed in.

Here’s the name element:

<label htmlFor="form-name">Name: </label>
<input
  id="form-name"
  type="text"
  value={name}
  onChange={(e) => {
	setName(e.target.value);
	setShowOutput(false);
  }}
  required
/>

Notice that we also use our showOutput setter, setting the value to false to that we hide a profile once it’s been modified.

Next is the title element, which looks very similar:

<label htmlFor="form-title">Title: </label>
<input
  id="form-title"
  type="text"
  value={title}
  onChange={(e) => {
	setTitle(e.target.value);
	setShowOutput(false);
  }}
  required
/>

The fun fact will need a larger text field, so we’ll use a textarea tag instead.

<label htmlFor="form-fun-fact" style={{ verticalAlign: "top" }}>
	Fun Fact:
</label>
<textarea
  id="form-fun-fact"
  name="w3review"
  value={fact}
  onChange={(e) => {
	setFact(e.target.value);
	setShowOutput(false);
  }}
></textarea>

The photo field will prove challenging, because we need to turn the URL into a photo we can display. We do this by accessing the file’s path from the event, creating a URL from it, and then by getting an object at that URL inside of your onChange:

<input
  id="member-photo"
  type="file"
  {/* no `value` because value is a path, but we want to store a photo */}
  onChange={(event) => {
    setPhoto(URL.createObjectURL(event.target.files[0]));
  }}
  required
/>

Once this is all complete, add these into the form component, separating each by a <br/> tag to create a separation. Then we can move to the output component.

Output

For the output, we need to display an image and text using the passed in properties:

export default function Output({ photo, name, title, fact }) {
  return (
    <div>
      <img src={photo ?? ""} alt="profile photo" />
      <h1>{name}</h1>
      <p>{title}</p>
      <p>Fun Fact:{fact}</p>
    </div>
  );
}

blocks.content: Now we have all of the pieces in place!

Touch-ups

It’s time to add some functionality details before we overhaul styling. First, we want to only display the output when showOutput is true. Add conditionality to the display of Output using a ternary operator:

{showOutput ? (<Output ... />) : (<></>)}

We can add this to the app component here:

// App.js
import { useState } from "react"; // required to use state
import Header from "./Header"; // import each component
import Form from "./Form";
import Output from "./Output";

export default function App() {
  // input field values
  const [photo, setPhoto] = useState(null);
  const [name, setName] = useState("");
  const [title, setTitle] = useState("");
  const [fact, setFact] = useState("");

  return (
    <div>
      <Header />
      <Form
		photo={photo} setPhoto={setPhoto}
		name={name} setName={setName}
		title={title} setTitle={setTitle}
		fact={fact} setFact={setFact}
		showOutput={showOutput} setShowOutput={setShowOutput}
	  />
      {showOutput ? (
	    <Output photo={photo} name={name} title={title} fact={fact}/>
      ) : (
        <></>
      )}
    </div>
  );
}

Styling

To complete this site, we need to make it look nice. To style the website, we need to add in some CSS. We won’t be covering the CSS principles here (you can read about that in CSS Basics), so below is the complete CSS file to add to your project. You can either download the file, or copy it from the block below.

div {
  padding: 10px;
  margin: 10px 0px;
  border-radius: 10px;
  background-color: #1e201a;
  color: #edf0f1;
  flex-flow: column;
}

div.input,
div.output {
  background-color: #2f4268;
  box-shadow: 0 0 10px #455c89;
  display: flex;
  justify-content: center;
  align-content: center;
  width: 400px;
  height: 200px;
}

div.output {
  background-color: #487268;
  box-shadow: 0 0 10px #689f92;
  flex-flow: row;
  margin-top: 20px;
}

div.column {
  background-color: inherit;
  margin: 0px;
  flex-flow: column;
  justify-content: center;
  align-content: center;
  justify-items: center;
  align-items: center;
}

label {
  font-weight: 700;
}

ul {
  margin-left: -30px;
  margin-bottom: -5px;
  margin-top: 10px;
  line-height: 0.8rem;
  list-style: none;
}

input,
textarea {
  border: 2px solid #dadada;
  border-radius: 4px;
  background: transparent;
  color: #edf0f1;
  margin: 5px 10px;
  font-family: "Roboto", sans-serif;
}

textarea {
  height: 40px;
  width: 175px;
}

input:focus,
textarea:focus {
  outline: none;
  border-color: #9ecaed;
  box-shadow: 0 0 10px #9ecaed;
}

input[type="submit"] {
  background-color: #edf0f1;
  color: #2f4268;
  font-weight: 700;
  font-size: larger;
}

input[type="file"] {
  background: transparent;
  border: transparent;
}

/* Import Roboto from Google Fonts */
@import url("<https://fonts.googleapis.com/css2?family=Roboto&display=swap>");
body {
  font-family: "Roboto", sans-serif;
  font-size: 1rem;
  background-color: #1e201a;
}

h1 {
  margin-top: 0px;
  margin-bottom: 0px;
}

img {
  border-radius: 10px;
  box-shadow: 0 0 10px #689f92;
  object-fit: cover;
  width: 180px;
  height: 180px;
}

Drop this into the src directory, and we’re good to go! Open up your terminal and run the command npm start.

One option we have for extending this is to add a backend to this frontend-only project. If we wanted to automatically build these profiles based on a roster of Oasis members, we can connect to an API to get this information.

To go down this route, check out Building a Restful API and Going Full Stack.

New Functionality

An alternative is to add new functionality. One option here is to add the ability to generate and show multiple profiles at a time. Let’s consider what this would require.

First, we need to rethink how we store our data. While we still need our current state variables to store the information for the profile we’re working on, we need to store all past profiles in a list. Instead of the output taking all of our inputs, it will now only take our list of completed profiles. The form will also need the profiles and the profiles setter so that it can update the list.

// App.js
import { useState } from "react"; // required to use state
import Header from "./Header"; // import each component
import Form from "./Form";
import Output from "./Output";

export default function App() {
  // input field values
  const [photo, setPhoto] = useState(null);
  const [name, setName] = useState("");
  const [title, setTitle] = useState("");
  const [fact, setFact] = useState("");
  
  // add a list of profiles
  const [profiles, setProfiles] = useState([]);

  const [showOutput, setShowOutput] = useState(false);

	return (
    <div>
      <Header />
      <Form
		photo={photo} setPhoto={setPhoto}
		name={name} setName={setName}
		title={title} setTitle={setTitle}
		fact={fact} setFact={setFact}
		showOutput={showOutput} setShowOutput={setShowOutput}
		profiles={profiles} setProfiles={setProfiles}
	  />
      {showOutput ? (
	    <Output photo={photo} name={name} title={title} fact={fact}/>
      ) : (
        <></>
      )}
    </div>
	);
}

Next, we want the output to be shown when we have at least 1 completed profile. To do this, we’ll start by removing the showOutput state value. We’ll then only render the output if the length of our list of profiles is at least 1.

// App.js
import { useState } from "react"; // required to use state
import Header from "./Header"; // import each component
import Form from "./Form";
import Output from "./Output";

export default function App() {
  // input field values
  const [photo, setPhoto] = useState(null);
  const [name, setName] = useState("");
  const [title, setTitle] = useState("");
  const [fact, setFact] = useState("");
  
  // add a list of profiles
  const [profiles, setProfiles] = useState([]);

	return (
    <div>
      <Header />
      <Form
		photo={photo} setPhoto={setPhoto}
		name={name} setName={setName}
		title={title} setTitle={setTitle}
		fact={fact} setFact={setFact}
		profiles={profiles} setProfiles={setProfiles}
	  />
      {profiles.length > 0 && 
	    <Output photo={photo} name={name} title={title} fact={fact} />
      }
    </div>
	);
}

Next, we’ll modify our form. We start by removing any remnants of showOutput and setShowOutput, and adding in the profiles and setProfiles arguments. Then, we want to modify out form tag, changing the onSubmit to append the current profile to the list of created profiles. This new tag will look like the following:

<form
  onSubmit={(e) => {
	e.preventDefault(); 
	var newProfile = {
	  photo: photo, // remember that these refer to our state values
	  name: name, 
	  title: title, 
	  fact: fact 
  }
    // concatonate the new profile to our current list
    var newProfilesList = profiles.concat(newProfile)
    setProfiles(newProfilesList) 
  }}
>

Finally, we can modify our output to produce several profiles, instead of just the one. Using our new profiles argument, we can use Javascript’s map function, which can produce HTML for each item in a list. We can put our old output code into this map to make a card for each profile.

export default function Output({ profiles }) {
  return (
    <div>
      {profiles.map((profile) => (
        <div className="output">
          <div className="column">
            <img src={profile.photo ?? ""} alt="profile photo" />
          </div>

          <div className="column">
            <h1 style={{ marginBottom: "-15px", marginTop: "2px" }}>
              {profile.name ?? "error"}
            </h1>
            <p>
              <b>
                <i>{profile.title ?? "error"}</i>
              </b>
            </p>
            <p>
              <b>Fun Fact:</b>
              <br /> {profile.fact ?? "error"}
            </p>
          </div>
        </div>
      ))}
    </div>
  );
}

With that completed, we can run our application and try to make multiple profiles. Now I can compare two profiles to see which one I like best!
